Chapter 6 210
Multi-stage reviews
Access reviews support up to three review stages. This enables multiple approvers to review
access to idx_fa931a08 resources before a decision is made. It helps organizations meet certification and
audit requirements, design more efficient reviews, and reduce the number of decisions each
reviewer is responsible for.
Multi-stage idx_218dc683 reviews help meet the following use cases:
Reach consensus across multiple reviewers: This might be useful when access to
highly critical resources is being reviewed or when there is a diverse set of reviewees,
and it is hard for a single reviewer to make the decision.
Get input on unreviewed decisions: If the first stage approvers are unable to decide,
second stage and third stage reviewers can help.
Reduce burden on later-stage reviewers: Reviews can be configured in such a way
that if a deny decision is made at an earlier stage, those users are not reviewed at the
later stages. This way the subsequent stage approvers see a filtered down list.
The options idx_b54086ae available while configuring multi-stage review are:
Reviewers: Group owners, selected users or groups, users themselves, or managers of
users can be configured as reviewers. For group owners, selected users or groups and
managers of users, fallback reviewers can be configured. These will be used if primary
reviewers do not exist.
Stage duration: This specifies the number of days within which reviewers at each
stage must respond to the review request.
Show previous stage(s) decision to later stage reviewers: You can choose to reveal or
hide the decision taken by earlier stage reviewers by selecting or deselecting this box.
Review recurrence: You can specify if the access review is one time or recurring. The
available options are One time, Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly, Semi-annually, and
Annually. If you choose a recurring review, you can specify start date and end options
like Never, End on specific date, or End after number of occurrences.
Reviewees going to next stage: Lastly, you can choose to send all or only a subset of
reviewees to the next stage. The available options are All, Approved reviewees,
Denied reviewees, Not reviewed reviewees, and Reviewees marked as "Don't
know".

In this chapter, you explored the fundamentals of Microsoft Entra ID Governance, with a
specific focus on the principle of least privilege—ensuring users have only the necessary

7
Microsoft Entra Lifecycle
Workflows
Lifecycle workflows play a critical role in modern identity and access management by
streamlining and automating the processes associated with a user's journey within an
organization. From the moment a new employee joins (the joiner), through internal changes
such as promotions or department transfers (the mover), to when they leave the company (the
leaver), each stage demands precise updates to access rights and group memberships to
maintain both productivity and security. Manual management of these transitions is not only
time-consuming but also prone to errors, which can lead to unauthorized access or overlooked
permissions, posing significant security risks.
By leveraging lifecycle workflows, organizations can ensure that user accounts are provisioned,
updated, and deprovisioned automatically and consistently. This automation supports
compliance with regulatory requirements by providing clear audit trails of access changes and
minimizing the risk of data breaches due to lingering or excessive permissions. Additionally,
lifecycle workflows improve operational efficiency by reducing the administrative burden on IT
teams, allowing them to focus on more strategic initiatives. The use of predefined templates
and integration with HR tools further accelerates deployment and ensures that the workflows
reflect organizational policies and best practices.
This chapter will cover:
Introduction to Microsoft Entra Lifecycle Workflows
LCW and Zero Trust
Create and manage lifecycle workflows
•
•
•
Introduction to Microsoft Entra Lifecycle Workflows
Lifecycle Workflows (LCW) is a feature in Microsoft Entra ID Governance that enables
organizations idx_0bb3f8c4 to manage users by automating the lifecycle processes of joiner, mover, and
leaver. Workflows contain processes that run automatically for users as they move through the
identity lifecycle.
Organizations idx_80723632 that want to modernize their identity lifecycle management process need to
ensure that users have the correct access to the correct resources, groups, and applications on
the day they join the organization. They also must ensure that access is revoked in a timely
manner for users who have left the organization. It is also important that the process of
provisioning and revoking access is not overly complicated and time-consuming for
administrators. Administrators should also be able to troubleshoot problems and have access
to logs that help with troubleshooting, audit, and compliance.
There are several reasons why an organization would like to use lifecycle workflows. Some of

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 224
chunks.content:
the key ones are as follows:
Extend the HR-driven provisioning process with other workflows to simplify and
automate tasks.
Centralize the workflow process to be able to create and manage all workflows in one
location.
Troubleshoot workflow scenarios using audit logs and workflow history.
Manage the identity and access management lifecycle at scale.
Automate manual tasks.
Use logic apps to extend the capability for more complex scenarios.
The capabilities in lifecycle workflows help remove dependencies and increase efficiency in
new employee onboarding and offboarding of former employees.
•
•
•
•
•
•

LCW are best suited for the following scenarios:
Automatic user provisioning from HR tools: For most organizations, a relationship
with a idx_62db33f6 new employee begins by onboarding them to their Human Resource
Management System (HRMS). These user identities must then be created in
Microsoft Entra for the new employees to be able to access the IT systems. Using LCW,
organizations can automate onboarding tasks like account creation, generating
temporary passwords, and sending emails.
Automate dynamic group membership: Organizations that have well defined groups
can automate user membership of those groups. Lifecycle workflows are different from
dynamic groups in the following ways:
They can manage static groups, so you don't need to manage dynamic group
rules.
You are not limited to one rule per group. Lifecycle workflow rules determine the
scope of users against whom the workflow is executed.
Attributes beyond the ones supported by dynamic groups are available. For
example, employeeHireDate.
Lifecycle workflows can perform actions on groups, and not just membership.
Workflow history and audit: An audit trail of the user lifecycle process can be created.
Automate user account management: Lifecycle workflows can help ensure that users
who idx_f7a4c913 are leaving the organization have their access revoked in a timely manner.
Automate access package assignment: Using lifecycle workflows, access packages
can be automatically assigned and removed based on user attribute changes.
Logic apps integration: Lifecycle workflows can be integrated with logic apps for
more complex scenarios.
Microsoft Entra provides predefined templates ready for use by the administrator. This helps
with quicker deployment of workflows. The following screenshot shows examples of these
templates:

Most idx_8f7f25ed workflows require that certain conditions be met for them to execute. These conditions
are called triggers. Some are on-demand workflows and do not use a trigger.
LCW as a Zero Trust control
The Zero Trust security model operates on three foundational principles: verify explicitly, use
least-privilege access, and assume breach. In environments where identity has replaced the
network idx_d4a68714 perimeter as the primary control plane, these principles demand that every user
account be continuously validated, scoped to the minimum necessary permissions, and treated
as a potential vector for compromise.
LCW provides the automation framework that translates these Zero Trust principles into
operational reality. By orchestrating identity actions across the joiner-mover-leaver cycle,
LCW ensures that access is granted, adjusted, and revoked in a timely, policy-driven manner,

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 228
chunks.content:
eliminating the manual gaps that attackers exploit.
Every active identity in a directory represents a potential entry point for an attacker. The
identity attack surface grows not only with the number of accounts, but also with the
privileges those accounts hold and the duration for which those privileges persist. Lifecycle
workflows reduce this surface across all three dimensions:
Account proliferation control: Joiner workflows ensure that accounts are created
through governed, template-driven processes with predefined group memberships,
•

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 230
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 230
license assignments, and access packages. This prevents the ad hoc account creation
that leads to ungoverned identities.
Privilege scoping: Mover workflows automatically adjust access when users change
roles, departments, or locations. Rather than accumulating permissions across job
changes, users receive only what their current role requires, enforcing the least-
privilege principle at every transition.
Timely deprovisioning: Leaver workflows disable accounts, revoke group
memberships, remove licenses, and schedule account deletion based on the
employeeLeaveDateTime attribute, ensuring that departing users cannot retain access
beyond their last day.
Together, these idx_0673be6f automated actions produce a continuously right-sized identity footprint.
Rather than relying on periodic manual reviews to discover and remediate over-provisioned or
stale accounts, LCW maintains hygiene as a continuous, event-driven process.
Let's explore how LCW acts as a Zero Trust control in each phase of the identity lifecycle.
Joiner phase
The joiner phase is where Zero Trust begins. New employees often wait days for access to the
tools they idx_d6e8927a need and when access finally arrives, it is frequently over-provisioned because
administrators grant broad permissions to avoid repeated requests.
LCW joiner workflows solve both problems simultaneously. By defining access packages tied to
specific roles and departments, the workflow grants exactly the permissions new employees
need, before their first day. This approach delivers immediate productivity while enforcing the
principle of least privilege from the moment the identity is created.
Pre-hire tasks can include generating a Temporary Access Pass, sending a welcome email with
onboarding instructions, and adding the user to their department's Microsoft Teams channels
and security groups. These tasks can be triggered automatically based on the
employeeHireDate attribute.
Mover phase
When users idx_b009163b change roles, they gradually accumulate permissions as their previous access is
seldom revoked. This privilege drift is one of the most persistent and insidious violations of the
least privilege principle. In organizations without mover automation, a user who moves from
finance to marketing may retain access to financial systems, sensitive reports, and
administrative tools that are no longer relevant to their role.
•
•
231 Microsoft Entra Lifecycle Workflows
Over time, these accumulated permissions create accounts with far more access than any
single role requires. These over-privileged accounts are prime targets for attackers because
compromising one account yields access to multiple organizational functions.
LCW mover idx_f7e2e0b9 workflows address privilege drift by automatically detecting attribute changes like

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 230
chunks.content:
updates to department or job title and executing a defined sequence of access adjustments.
Previous group memberships are removed, new role-appropriate access packages are assigned,
and the transition is logged for audit purposes. This approach enforces the principle of least
privilege access.
Leaver phase
The leaver phase represents the highest risk moment in the identity lifecycle from a Zero Trust
perspective. A departing employee's account, if left active, becomes an unmonitored identity
with valid idx_eacce20d credentials and established permissions. These serve as gold mines for attackers as
they can compromise these accounts and launch multi-stage attacks that can compromise
hybrid cloud environments, perform lateral movement, exfiltrate data, steal credentials, and
deploy ransomware in the environment.
Hybrid environments introduce a particular challenge for deprovisioning. When an employee
departs, their identity typically exists in multiple locations such as on-premises AD, Entra ID,
connected SaaS applications, and potentially downstream systems provisioned through SCIM
or custom connectors.
In organizations that rely on manual or ticket-based deprovisioning, the delay between an
employee's departure and the revocation of their access across all systems can range from days
to weeks. During that interval, the risk profile is severe. Even if the cloud account is disabled,
an on-premises AD account may remain active, providing access to file shares, VPN gateways,
and domain-joined resources. Applications provisioned outside the core identity platform may
not receive deprovisioning signals, leaving orphaned access in downstream systems.
LCW leaver workflows transform deprovisioning from a reactive, ticket-based process into a
deterministic, policy-driven operation. Whether triggered by the employeeLeaveDateTime
attribute for planned departures or executed on demand for immediate terminations, the
workflow ensures consistent, complete, and auditable offboarding across configured identity
systems. This approach enforces the principles of assume breach and least privilege access.
Lifecycle workflows are not merely an operational convenience. They are a foundational Zero
Trust idx_d54bd4d7 control. In an environment where identity is the perimeter, the hygiene of the identity
directory directly determines the organization's security posture. LCW ensures that:
Every identity is created with the minimum necessary permissions (verify explicitly,
least privilege).
•

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 232
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 232
Every role change triggers an automatic rebalancing of access (least privilege,
continuous verification).
Every departure results in timely, complete deprovisioning (assume breach, attack
surface reduction).
By automating the joiner–mover–leaver cycle, organizations move from a model of periodic,
manual identity governance to one of continuous, policy-driven enforcement.
Components of lifecycle workflows
Lifecycle idx_f80ee7a7 workflows contain processes that are executed against users as they move through
the identity lifecycle. Workflows consist of tasks and execution conditions. Execution
conditions consist of triggers and scope.
Tasks
Tasks are the idx_f8b9e53e specific actions that run automatically each time a workflow is triggered. Each
lifecycle workflow template contains several built-in tasks that are designed to automate
common lifecycle management scenarios. These tasks can also be used to build custom
workflows. Tasks are categorized based on the joiner-mover-leaver model so that
administrators can easily identify them and place them in appropriate workflows. These tasks
can send a welcome email to new employees, generate a Temporary Access Pass and email it to
the manager, add users to groups and Microsoft Teams, and do much more. In addition to
built-in tasks, custom task extensions can be used for more complex scenarios. The following
table lists the built-in tasks and their relevant scenarios:

Scope
Scope defines idx_84118315 who the workflow will affect. Depending on the triggers selected, the scope
options will change. This is explained as follows:
Time based attribute: When a time-based attribute trigger is selected, administrators
must define rules to determine the users who will be in scope of the workflow. The
scope query must contain the value of the attribute as it appears in the user object in
Entra ID. For example, department equals Marketing.
Attribute changes: Administrator must first select the attribute that will trigger the
workflow to run. The scope query must include the value of the attribute as it appears
in the user object in Entra ID. For example, department equals Marketing.
Group membership changes: The scope query must include the group from which the
user must be added or removed. Only one group can be selected at a time.
Sign in activity: Administrator must define rules to determine the users who will be in
scope of the workflow. For example, user type is Guest.
On-demand: For idx_1800578e on-demand workflows, administrators have the choice to select the
users while creating the workflow or when the workflow is run.
The scope should be carefully defined as it can directly affect the users.

Role requirements
A Global Administrator or Lifecycle Workflows Administrator Microsoft idx_5af1624a Entra role idx_da835983 is
required to create and manage idx_f2d08831 all aspects of workflows and tasks.
Licensing requirements
Using Lifecycle idx_397d67db workflows requires a Microsoft Entra ID Governance license. In addition, each
Lifecycle Workflow Administrator requires a license and each user who is in the scope of a
workflow requires a license.
Limits
Lifecycle idx_65972636 workflows are subject to certain limits as summarized in the following table:
Category Limit
Maximum number of workflows per tenant 100
Maximum number of tasks per workflow 25
Maximum number of custom task extensions per tenant 100

Keep in mind these limits while designing your lifecycle workflows. Now that we understand
the basics, let's proceed further.
Getting started with lifecycle workflows
Lifecycle workflows help organizations manage Microsoft Entra users efficiently by increasing
automation. Along with other Microsoft Entra ID Governance solutions such as entitlement
management, access reviews, and Privileged Identity Management, they help organizations
address key idx_8998eca6 access management questions. It is important to plan the deployment of lifecycle
workflows to achieve the desired governance strategy. Consider the organizational needs and
involve the right stakeholders to ensure that there are no mismatched expectations about
impact, outcomes, and responsibilities.
239 Microsoft Entra Lifecycle Workflows
Communication is often the key to the success of any new business process. Lifecycle
workflows shift responsibility for manual processes to business owners. It decouples the
onboarding and offboarding process from the IT department. This is a cultural shift and
requires accountability from resource owners. Therefore, proactive communication is
imperative, and resource owners must be trained to enable them to make the right decisions.
Prerequisites
Before an idx_af56407e organization starts creating and using lifecycle workflows, it is important to ensure
that the following technologies are in place:
Inbound provisioning
Most organizations have a process to create new employee records in their HRMS tool like
SuccessFactors idx_8014f0a9 or Workday. These employee records must be synchronized with Microsoft
Entra ID so that user accounts are auto provisioned. Microsoft Entra ID supports out-of-the-
box integration with SuccessFactors and Workday.
Microsoft Entra ID supports direct synchronization of user accounts from Workday and
SuccessFactors to on-premises Active Directory. Once the accounts are provisioned in on-
premises AD, they can be synchronized with Microsoft Entra ID using Microsoft Entra Connect

For organizations that use other systems of record, such as an HR app, a payroll app, a
spreadsheet, or a SQL database, Microsoft Entra ID supports API-driven provisioning.
Before starting off with lifecycle workflows, ensure that the user accounts are synchronized to
Microsoft Entra ID.
Attribute synchronization
Ensure idx_d2a5d0b1 that the accounts in Microsoft Entra ID have the employeeHireDate and
employeeLeaveDateTime attributes populated either manually or via HR provisioning.

The following attributes of an email can be customized: Recipients Sender domain Organizational branding Subject Message body Email language The default email template includes a security disclaimer. It is recommended to enable custom sender domain and organizational branding to remove this. If you choose to use the default email template, the text is automatically translated to the recipient's preferred language. If you specify a custom subject or body, the email is not translated. HTML formatting can be used to customize email text as follows: Bold the text by enclosing it within brackets. Italicize the text by enclosing it within brackets. Underline the text by enclosing it within brackets. Insert hyperlinks using brackets. In addition to the above, you can also personalize emails using dynamic attributes. Place dynamic attributes within emails to insert the user's name, manager's email, or their Temporary Access Pass. The correct format is {{dynamic attribute}}. We've already set up a few things to help you get started quickly and make your onboarding process as smooth as possible. For more information and next steps, please contact your manager, {{managerDisplayName}} To customize emails, follow the steps below: Login to https://entra.microsoft.com and navigate to ID Governance | Lifecycle workflows | Workflows. Custom task extensions
As we have learned, lifecycle workflows have several built-in tasks that can be used in various
joiner, mover, and leaver scenarios. These tasks may not be enough for some organizations.
Lifecycle idx_8d5a3940 workflows offers the flexibility to create custom task extensions to call external
systems as part of the workflow. For example, you may have a requirement that assigns the
ownership of a user's OneDrive account and mailbox to a manager when the user leaves the
organization. Lifecycle workflows use Azure Logic Apps to create these custom task extensions.
To use Azure Logic App to create a custom task extension you must have an Azure subscription
with a resource group. You must also have the required permissions to create a new
consumption-based Azure Logic App. You must have Logic App contributor, Contributor, or
Owner Azure role on the Logic App, or at the resource group, subscription, or management
group level.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 254
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 254
Custom task extensions interact with lifecycle workflows in one of the following two ways:
Launch and continue: If this is used when the workflow does not expect a response or
feedback from the Azure Logic App. If the Logic App started successfully, it is
considered a success. The next task in the workflow is immediately executed.
Launch and wait: This is used when the workflow requires a response from the Logic
App before executing the next task. A time duration is specified for how long the
workflow should wait for the Logic App to respond. If the Logic App does not respond
in that time frame, the task is considered failed.
When a custom extension waits for a response from a Logic App, the administrator can
define which application can send a response. The response can be sent by:
System-assigned managed identity: This is the default option and uses the
managed identity assigned to the Logic App.
No authorization: If using this option, administrators must manually assign
application permissions (LifecycleWorkflows.ReadWrite.All) or role
assignment (Lifecycle Workflows Administrator). This is not recommended as
this does not follow the principle of least privilege.
Existing application: Choose an existing application or a system or user-
assigned managed identity to respond.
The following idx_015178d6 are the high-level steps to use Azure Logic Apps with lifecycle workflows:
Create a consumption-based Azure Logic App.
Configure the Azure Logic App to be compatible with Lifecycle Workflows. Refer to
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-governance/configure-logic-
app-lifecycle-workflows.
Build the business logic within the Azure Logic App.
Create a lifecycle workflow custom extension to hold the information about the Azure
Logic App. Following are the detailed steps:
Login to https://entra.microsoft.com and navigate to ID Governance |
Lifecycle workflows | Custom extensions.
Click Add a custom extension.
On the Basics page, give a name and description for the custom extension. Click
Next: Task behavior.
Under the Task behavior tab, select the task behavior as either Launch and
continue or Launch and wait. Select the other options and click Next: Details.

Summary
In this chapter, we learned how we can use Lifecycle workflows to automate the identity
lifecycle across the joiner, mover and leaver scenarios. This chapter went deep into explaining

chunks.content:
Chapter 7 260
8
Microsoft Entra Privileged
Identity Management
Privileged identities are a critical component in modern security strategies, particularly for
organizations utilizing cloud and hybrid environments. These identities refer to accounts or
users that are granted elevated permissions, enabling them to perform sensitive operations,
such as managing user access, configuring systems, or administering critical resources.
Because these accounts hold the keys to an organization's most important assets, their
management must be robust, systematic, and auditable.
Effective management of privileged identities involves several best practices. Firstly, access
should be granted only when absolutely necessary, following the principle of least privilege.
This means limiting the scope and duration of elevated access, so that users only have the
necessary idx_216ef8f9 permissions for the task at hand and only for as long as needed. Microsoft Entra
Privileged Identity Management (PIM) facilitates this by providing just-in-time and time-
bound access, requiring approval workflows, and enforcing multi-factor authentication for role
activation. Additionally, regular access reviews and justification requests ensure that privileges
are not retained longer than required, reducing the risk of misuse or compromise.
By centralizing and automating the management of privileged identities, organizations can
significantly reduce their attack surface, maintain compliance with regulatory requirements,
and improve overall security posture.
This chapter will cover:
Introduction to privileged identities
Deploying Privileged Identity Management
Managing Privileged Identity Management
Auditing PIM
Introduction to privileged identities
Privileged identities are specialized accounts or users within an organization that have been
granted elevated permissions, allowing them to perform critical and sensitive operations that
go beyond idx_1a49506e what standard users can do. These identities are central to the administration of IT
systems, cloud services, and data resources because they have the authority to manage user
access, configure infrastructure, oversee system security, and even alter or delete vital data. In a
modern business environment the concept of privileged identities has become a cornerstone in
the defense against cyber threats and the assurance of regulatory compliance.
Service accounts used by applications to access databases or perform automated tasks may
also be considered privileged if they are granted broad access rights. Because these identities
hold the "keys to the kingdom," they are highly attractive targets for cyber attackers. If
compromised, a privileged account can be used to escalate attacks, exfiltrate sensitive data, or
disrupt business operations on a large scale.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 260
chunks.content:
Managing privileged identities effectively is critical. The management of privileged identities
involves several key strategies. First, access to privileged roles should be time-bound and just-
in-time. Instead of granting permanent elevated access, organizations should provide
privileged access only when it is needed and for a limited duration. Microsoft Entra
Privileged Identity Management (PIM) automates this process by allowing users to activate
privileged roles only after passing additional checks or approval workflows. These controls
ensure that access is not only temporary but also auditable, providing a clear record of who
accessed what resources and when.
In summary, privileged identities are essential but high-risk. Strong controls are essential to
protect critical systems and minimize an organization's attack surface.
Now that we understand privileged accounts and their importance, let's explore Microsoft
Entra Privileged Identity Management.

Chapter 8 262
Overview of Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity
Management
Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) is a service that enables
organizations to idx_f812f14c manage, control and monitor access to important resources like Microsoft
Entra ID, Azure and other Microsoft Online services like Microsoft Intune and Microsoft 365.
PIM provides time-based and approval-based role activation that minimizes the risk of
excessive, unnecessary or misused access permissions on resources.
Organizations want to restrict the number of users that have privileged access to prevent a bad
actor from getting that access or an authorized user inadvertently or maliciously misusing the
access. However, IT admins still need privileges to carry out privileged operations in Microsoft
idx_cc922016 Entra ID, Azure or Microsoft 365. Using PIM organizations can give admins just-in-time access
to resources and oversee what they are doing with that access.
The following idx_922f1294 are some key features of PIM:
It provides just-in-time access to Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources
It provides time-bound access to resources
It can require approval to activate privileged roles
It can enforce MFA to activate privileged roles
It can ask for justification to activate the privileged role
Access reviews can be conducted to ensure users still need the roles
Notifications can be sent when privileged roles are activated
Audit history is maintained for internal or external audits
Access to the following resources can be controlled using PIM:
Microsoft Entra roles: Access to both built-in and custom roles can be managed using
PIM. All Microsoft 365 roles like Exchange Administrator and SharePoint Administrator
can be managed by PIM. However, service specific roles within Exchange RBAC or
SharePoint RBAC are not supported.
Azure resource roles: These include built-in and custom roles that grant access to
management groups, subscriptions, resources groups and resources in Azure. Classic
subscription administrator roles like Account Administrator, Service Administrator and
Co-Administrator cannot be managed using PIM.
Groups: Using PIM just-in-time access can be set up to assign users as members or
owners of a Microsoft Entra security group or a Microsoft 365 group.

It is idx_503950b6 recommended to have zero permanently active members for roles other than two cloud-

Emergency access accounts
Organizations need to ensure that administrators are not accidentally locked out of Microsoft
Entra idx_8fc6cd0b because they cannot sign in or activate a role. This can be done by creating emergency
access accounts. These idx_53945754 accounts, also called break glass accounts, are limited to emergency
scenarios where normal administrative accounts cannot be used.
Break glass accounts may be required in the following situations:
The user accounts are federated from on-premises Active Directory and federation is
unavailable.
The administrators are registered to use MFA, and devices are unavailable or the service
is unavailable.
•
•
265 Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management
The last Global Administrator left the organization. While Microsoft Entra ID prevents
the deletion of the last Global Administrator account, it can still be disabled or deleted
on-premises.
Natural disasters due to which cellular or other services are unavailable.
If activating the Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator role requires
approval and no approvers are assigned or all approvers are removed from the
directory.
Follow the steps below to create an emergency access account. These should be cloud-only
accounts that use the *.onmicrosoft.com domain and are not synchronized from on-premises
Active Directory.
Create a new user account and permanently assign the Global Administrator role.
Select a passwordless authentication method like Passkey or certificate-based
authentication to satisfy the mandatory MFA requirements.
Configure the emergency account to use the assigned passwordless authentication
method.
Create a Conditional Access policy to require phishing resistant MFA for the emergency
accounts.
Store account credentials safely.
Regularly monitor the sign-in and audit logs for any unusual activity on these
accounts.
Validate the accounts regularly.

In most idx_da65e0bc organizations, emergency access accounts are not associated with any user.
Credentials are set to never expire and are stored in a secure location known to multiple
members of the IT staff. These accounts are not connected to employee devices. A secure access
workstation must be used to use these accounts.
Role assignment overview

complete an associated task. An approver reviews this request and approves or rejects it. The
requestor completes the task. If required, the requestor can extend or renew their access. The
